title: Sum of Good Subsequences
statement:
A subsequence of the integer array `nums` keeps one or more of its elements in their original order. Call a subsequence **good** when every two neighbouring elements in it differ by exactly `1` (in either direction); a subsequence with a single element is always good.

Take every good subsequence, counting subsequences built from different index sets separately even when their values match, and add up all of their elements. Return that grand total modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing all `2^n` subsequences is far too slow. But a good subsequence can only grow by a value one above or one below its last element, so its last value is all that matters for the future. Group the good subsequences found so far by their last value `v` and keep two numbers per group: how many there are, `count`, and the sum of all their elements, `total`. A new element `x` extends every subsequence ending in `x − 1` or `x + 1`, and also starts one of its own.

## Approach

1. Keep two maps keyed by last value, `count` and `total`, both modulo `10^9 + 7`.
2. For each `x` in `nums`, the good subsequences ending at this element are `[x]` plus one extension of each subsequence ending in `x − 1` or `x + 1`: `ways = 1 + below + above`.
3. Their elements sum to the extended sums, `carried = total[x − 1] + total[x + 1]`, plus one `x` per new subsequence: `added = carried + ways · x`.
4. Add `ways` to `count[x]` and `added` to `total[x]`.
5. Return the sum of every value in `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 1]`.

- `x = 1`: nothing to extend, `ways = 1`, `added = 1` (just `[1]`). Now `count[1] = 1`, `total[1] = 1`.
- `x = 2`: `below = 1`, so `ways = 2`; `carried = 1` and `added = 1 + 2·2 = 5` (`[2]`, `[1,2]`). Now `count[2] = 2`, `total[2] = 5`.
- `x = 1`: `above = 2`, so `ways = 3`; `carried = 5` and `added = 5 + 3·1 = 8` (`[1]`, `[2,1]`, `[1,2,1]`). Now `total[1] = 9`.

The answer is `9 + 5 = 14`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): a constant number of map operations per element.
- Space: O(d) for the `d` distinct values.

## Pitfalls

- Equal neighbours do not count: `[2, 2]` is not good, so never extend subsequences that end in `x` itself.
- Appending `x` adds it to *each* extended subsequence, so the new sum is `carried + ways · x`, not `carried + x`.
- Values can be `0`; looking up `x − 1 = −1` just finds nothing.
- Reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` throughout; `ways · x` stays below 2^53 only because `ways` is reduced.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | last value → number of good subsequences so far that end in it |
| `total` | last value → sum of all elements of those subsequences |
| `x` | the current element |
| `below`, `above` | counts ending in `x − 1` and `x + 1` |
| `ways` | good subsequences that end at this element |
| `carried` | element sum of the subsequences being extended |
| `added` | element sum of all good subsequences ending at this element |
| `answer` | the sum of every value in `total` |

narration.3: count maps a last value to how many good subsequences seen so far end in it.
narration.4: total maps a last value to the sum of all elements of those subsequences.
narration.6: Process the elements in order; each can only be appended to subsequences of earlier elements.
narration.7: Subsequences ending one below x can take x next...
narration.8: ...and so can those ending one above x.

narration.10: The extended subsequences bring their existing element sums along.
narration.11: Each new subsequence also contains x itself, once per subsequence.
narration.12: Record the new subsequences under their last value x.
narration.13: Add their element sum to x's total as well.
narration.16: Every good subsequence ends in exactly one value, so summing the totals counts each of them once.
narration.17: Visit the stored total of every last value.
narration.18: Fold that group in, keeping the result reduced.
narration.20: Return the sum over all good subsequences.
